# (PART) LLM Foundations {-}

# Foundations of Generative AI and LLMs {#foundations-of-generative-ai-and-llms}

This part of the book builds an understanding of large language models from
the ground up, following the lifecycle of an LLM project:

| Chapter | Question it answers |
|:--------|:--------------------|
| This chapter | What is an LLM, how does a transformer generate text, and how do prompts and generation settings shape the output? |
| Chapter \@ref(pre-training-and-scaling-large-language-models) | How are LLMs pre-trained, and what do model size, data, and compute buy? |
| Chapter \@ref(instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation) | How do we adapt a model to our tasks, efficiently, and measure the result? |
| Chapter \@ref(alignment-human-feedback) | How do we make a model helpful, honest, and harmless? |
| Chapter \@ref(llm-applications) | How do we serve a model and connect it to data and tools responsibly? |

These chapters began as study notes from the DeepLearning.AI / AWS course
*Generative AI with Large Language Models* (Coursera). They have since been
rewritten as a reference, checked against the primary papers cited in each
chapter, and extended with later developments.

## What generative AI is

**Generative models** learn the statistical structure of their training data
and produce new samples from it: text, images, audio, video, or code. This
book focuses on **large language models (LLMs)**: neural networks trained on
very large text corpora to predict the next token. Chatbots, code assistants,
and writing tools are applications built on top of that one capability.

Key terms:

- **Foundation model.** A model trained broadly enough to be adapted to many
  downstream tasks. Examples include BERT, GPT, T5/FLAN-T5, BLOOM, and Llama.
  Its capabilities must be measured on each task; they cannot be assumed from
  its size.
- **Parameters.** The learned weights, currently up to hundreds of billions
  for large models. Parameters encode distributed statistical patterns, *not*
  a database of retrievable facts. More parameters add capacity, but data,
  training recipe, and adaptation matter as much.
- **Prompt, completion, inference.** The text you send is the *prompt*.
  Producing text is *inference*. The output is the *completion*.
- **Context window.** The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at
  once: instructions, conversation, documents, tool results, and its own
  output. The limit varies by model; check current documentation.

You interact with an LLM in natural language, not in a formal programming
language. You can use it as is, or adapt it (Chapter
\@ref(instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation)) without training a new model.

> **In short.**
>
> - An LLM is a neural network trained on huge text corpora to predict the
>   next token; chatbots and assistants are applications built on that.
> - Parameters store statistical patterns, not a fact database.
> - The context window caps everything the model can see at once.

## What LLMs are used for

Many tasks reduce to next-token prediction under the right prompt:

- **Generation**: drafting essays, emails, or marketing copy.
- **Summarization**: condensing dialogues, documents, or reviews.
- **Translation**: between natural languages, or from natural language to code
  or SQL.
- **Information extraction**: pulling named entities (people, places,
  organizations), fields, or labels out of text.
- **Augmented tasks**: answering from documents or calling APIs. These are not
  abilities of the model alone; the surrounding application supplies the data
  and tools (Chapter \@ref(llm-applications)).

Larger models generally handle more tasks without examples. Smaller or
specialized models can still be the better choice on cost, latency, privacy,
or a narrow task. Choose by evaluating on your own use case.

> **In short.**
>
> - Generation, summarization, translation, and extraction are all
>   next-token prediction under the right prompt.
> - Answering from documents or calling APIs needs an application around the
>   model.
> - Pick the model size by evaluation, not by default.

## Before transformers: recurrent networks

Earlier language models used **recurrent neural networks (RNNs)**. An RNN
reads tokens one at a time and carries a hidden state forward, so in principle
it summarizes everything seen so far. In practice it has three problems:

- **Long-range dependencies.** Gradients shrink (or explode) as they flow back
  through many time steps, so plain RNNs struggle to learn from distant
  context [@bengio1994vanishing]. LSTMs reduced but did not remove the problem
  [@hochreiter1997lstm].
- **Sequential computation.** Step $t$ needs the result of step $t-1$. Training
  cannot be parallelized across positions, which limits model and data scale.
- **A fixed-size bottleneck.** The whole history must be squeezed into one
  state vector.

Language needs wide context. Words have several meanings: a *bank* can be a
financial institution or a riverside. Sentences can be syntactically
ambiguous: in "The teacher taught the students with the book", whose book is
it? Resolving such cases often requires the whole sentence or document.

**Attention** was the fix. It was first added to RNN translation models: the
decoder learned to look back at all encoder states and weight the most
relevant ones [@bahdanau2015attention]. The transformer took the next step and
dropped recurrence entirely.

> **In short.**
>
> - RNNs read one token at a time: weak on long-range context, impossible to
>   parallelize across positions, and limited by one state vector.
> - Attention lets the model look back at all earlier states directly.

## The transformer

"Attention Is All You Need" [@vaswani2017attention] introduced the
**transformer**. It is built from attention and position-wise feed-forward
layers, with no recurrence. Two properties explain its success:

- **Parallelism.** All positions in a sequence are processed at once. That
  makes training efficient on GPUs and allows much larger models and datasets.
- **Direct context.** Every token can attend to every other token in one
  step, however far apart they are.

### From text to vectors

1. **Tokenization.** Text is split into **tokens** from a fixed vocabulary.
   Tokens are usually subword units learned by algorithms such as byte-pair
   encoding [@sennrich2016bpe], so rare words split into pieces. Each token
   maps to an integer ID. A model must always be used with the tokenizer it
   was trained with. For example, a tokenizer might split "unbelievably" into
   `un` + `believ` + `ably`, while "the" is a single token (the exact split
   depends on the tokenizer). For English, a common rule of thumb is about
   0.75 words per token, so 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words.
2. **Embedding.** Each token ID is mapped to a learned vector of dimension
   $d_{\text{model}}$ (512 in the original transformer). Tokens with related
   meanings end up close together in this space.
3. **Positional information.** Attention by itself ignores order, so position
   must be added. The original paper added fixed sinusoidal **positional
   encodings** to the embeddings. Many modern LLMs instead use rotary position
   embeddings (RoPE), which encode relative position inside the attention
   computation [@su2024rope].

### Self-attention

Each token's vector $x_i$ is projected into three vectors with learned
matrices. The **query** $q_i = x_i W^Q$ says what the token is looking for.
The **key** $k_j = x_j W^K$ says what each token offers. The **value**
$v_j = x_j W^V$ is what gets passed along if the token is attended to.
Stacking these vectors into matrices $Q, K, V$ gives **scaled dot-product
attention**:

$$
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
$$

- $QK^\top$ scores how relevant every token is to every other token. The
  softmax turns each row of scores into weights that sum to one; plotted as a
  grid, these weights form an **attention map**. Each output is a weighted
  average of the value vectors.
- **Why divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$?** Dot products grow with the vector dimension
  $d_k$. Large scores push the softmax towards a one-hot output, where
  gradients become very small. Scaling keeps training stable.
- **Multi-head attention** runs $h$ attention operations in parallel, each
  with its own projections (the original used $h = 8$ heads of size
  $d_k = 64$), and concatenates the results. Different heads learn
  different relations, for example syntactic agreement, coreference, or
  topic. Which relation a head learns is not chosen in advance.
- **Cost.** The score matrix is $n \times n$ for a sequence of $n$ tokens, so
  attention compute and memory grow **quadratically** with context length.
  That is why long contexts are expensive. At 4,096 tokens the matrix has
  about 16.8 million entries per head and layer; at 131,072 tokens (32 times
  longer) it has about 17.2 billion, 1,024 times more. Optimized kernels
  such as FlashAttention avoid storing the full matrix, but the compute
  still grows quadratically.

**Example: one attention step.** In "The campaign missed its target because
it launched late", the token "it" should attend mostly to "campaign".
Suppose its scaled scores against "campaign", "target", and "late" are 2.0,
0.0, and 1.0. The softmax turns them into weights of about 0.67, 0.09, and
0.24. The output for "it" is then $0.67\,v_{\text{campaign}} +
0.09\,v_{\text{target}} + 0.24\,v_{\text{late}}$: a vector that now carries
mostly the meaning of "campaign". (Real models attend over every token, and
each head produces its own weights.)

### The rest of a transformer block

Each layer (block) wraps attention with:

- a **position-wise feed-forward network**: two linear layers with a
  nonlinearity, applied to each token separately (inner width 2,048 in the
  original);
- **residual connections** and **layer normalization** around both
  sub-layers, which make deep stacks trainable.

The original model stacked six such layers in the encoder and six in the
decoder. A final linear layer maps each output vector to one **logit** per
vocabulary token, and a **softmax** turns the logits into a probability
distribution over the next token.

### Encoder, decoder, and the three model families

- The **encoder** reads the whole input with *bidirectional* self-attention.
  It produces a contextual representation of each input token.
- The **decoder** generates output one token at a time. Its self-attention is
  *masked* (causal): each position sees only earlier positions, so the model
  cannot peek at the token it is predicting. In an encoder–decoder model, the
  decoder also uses **cross-attention**, where its queries attend over the
  encoder's outputs.

Using one or both halves gives three families: **encoder-only** (BERT),
**decoder-only** (GPT, Llama), and **encoder–decoder** (T5, BART). They differ
in pre-training objective and in which tasks they suit. Chapter
\@ref(pre-training-and-scaling-large-language-models) compares them in
detail.

### Generating text, end to end

Take translation with an encoder–decoder model, from "J'aime l'apprentissage
automatique" to "I love machine learning":

1. Tokenize the French sentence with the model's tokenizer.
2. The **encoder** processes all input tokens in parallel into contextual
   representations.
3. The **decoder** starts from a start-of-sequence token. Attending to its own
   previous outputs and (through cross-attention) to the encoder's
   representations, it produces a distribution over the next token, and one
   token is chosen.
4. The chosen token is appended and fed back in. Step 3 repeats until an
   end-of-sequence token is produced or a length limit is reached.
5. **Detokenize** the output tokens into text.

A decoder-only model works the same way without the encoder. The prompt and
the tokens generated so far form one sequence, and the model extends it one
token at a time. This loop is **autoregressive** generation. How the next
token is *chosen* from the distribution is set by the generation
configuration (Section \@ref(configuring-generative-ai-models)).

### Landmark models

| Model | Year | Family | Size | Why it matters |
|:------|:-----|:-------|:-----|:---------------|
| BERT [@devlin2019bert] | 2018 | Encoder | 110M (Base), 340M (Large) | Bidirectional pre-training with masked language modelling; set the pattern of pre-train then fine-tune for understanding tasks |
| T5 [@raffel2020t5] | 2019 | Encoder–decoder | Up to 11B | Framed every task as text-to-text; FLAN-T5 is its instruction-tuned version |
| GPT-3 [@brown2020gpt3] | 2020 | Decoder | 175B | Showed strong few-shot in-context learning at scale |
| BLOOM [@bigscience2022bloom] | 2022 | Decoder | 176B | Open-science, multilingual (46 natural and 13 programming languages) |
| LLaMA [@touvron2023llama] | 2023 | Decoder | 7B–65B | Smaller models trained on more tokens; led a wave of open-weight models |

Model families move quickly. Use this table for the historical milestones, and
check current model cards for anything newer.

> **In short.**
>
> - Tokens become embeddings plus position information.
> - Self-attention, $\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$, lets every token
>   take a weighted average of every other token's values; multi-head runs
>   several in parallel; cost is quadratic in length.
> - Encoder (bidirectional), decoder (causal), encoder–decoder
>   (cross-attention); generation is autoregressive, one token at a time.

## Prompting and in-context learning {#prompt-engineering}

**Prompt engineering** is designing the input so the model produces the
desired completion. Its most important effect, discovered at scale, is
**in-context learning (ICL)**: the model picks up a task from examples placed
in the prompt, with no weight updates [@brown2020gpt3].

- **Zero-shot:** an instruction and the input, no examples. For example,
  "Classify this review: … Sentiment:".
- **One-shot:** one solved example before the real input.
- **Few-shot:** several solved examples, ideally covering the label space (for
  example, both a positive and a negative review).

A few-shot prompt for tagging customer comments:

```text
Tag each comment as PRICE, DELIVERY, or PRODUCT.

Comment: "Arrived three days late and the box was crushed."
Tag: DELIVERY

Comment: "Great jacket, but $40 more than at the outlet."
Tag: PRICE

Comment: "The zipper broke after one week."
Tag:
```

The model continues with "PRODUCT". The examples teach both the labels and
the output format, without any training.

What to know:

- **ICL depends on scale.** Large models often do well zero-shot. Small models
  may fail even with several examples.
- **Examples cost context.** They use up the context window and add tokens to
  every call.
- **There is a ceiling.** If a handful of examples does not get the
  performance you need, more examples rarely help. That is the signal to
  fine-tune (Chapter \@ref(instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation)).

The Prompt Engineering part of this book (starting with Chapter
\@ref(prompt-anatomy)) covers prompt structure, techniques, and evaluation in
depth.

> **In short.**
>
> - In-context learning: the model picks up a task from examples in the
>   prompt, with no weight updates.
> - Zero-, one-, and few-shot differ only in the number of solved examples.
> - It depends on scale and costs context; if a few examples do not work,
>   fine-tune.

## Configuring generation {#configuring-generative-ai-models}

At each step the model outputs a probability distribution over the
vocabulary. **Inference-time settings** (as opposed to training parameters)
decide how the next token is picked from it, and when to stop.

- **Max new tokens.** A cap on the number of generated tokens. Generation can
  stop earlier at an end-of-sequence token.
- **Greedy decoding.** Always pick the most probable token. It is
  deterministic and fine for short factual outputs, but prone to repetitive
  loops in longer text. (*Beam search*, which keeps the best few partial
  sequences, is a deterministic alternative common in translation.)
- **Random sampling.** Draw the next token in proportion to its probability.
  This adds variety but can wander into low-probability, incoherent tokens.
  In Hugging Face Transformers, sampling is enabled with `do_sample=True`.
- **Top-k sampling.** Sample only from the $k$ most probable tokens,
  renormalized.
- **Top-p (nucleus) sampling.** Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose
  cumulative probability reaches $p$. The candidate set adapts to how
  confident the model is [@holtzman2020nucleus].
- **Temperature.** Rescale the logits before the softmax:
  $p_i \propto \exp(z_i / T)$. $T < 1$ sharpens the distribution (more
  predictable). $T > 1$ flattens it (more varied). $T = 1$ leaves it
  unchanged.

**Worked example.** Suppose the next-token logits are apple $= -1.0$,
banana $= 0.5$, cake $= 2.0$, and donut $= 1.2$.

| Next token | $T = 0.5$ | $T = 1.0$ | $T = 2.0$ |
|:-----------|--------:|--------:|--------:|
| apple      | 0.002   | 0.029   | 0.094   |
| banana     | 0.040   | 0.130   | 0.200   |
| cake       | 0.797   | 0.581   | 0.423   |
| donut      | 0.161   | 0.261   | 0.283   |

At $T = 1$:

- **Top-k with $k = 3$** keeps cake, donut, and banana and renormalizes them
  to 0.598, 0.269, and 0.133.
- **Top-p with $p = 0.8$** keeps cake and donut, the smallest set whose
  cumulative probability (0.842) reaches 0.8, and renormalizes them to 0.690
  and 0.310.

Apple can never be sampled under either filter.

In practice, use low temperature or greedy decoding for extraction,
classification, and code. Use moderate temperature with top-p for open-ended
writing. Hosted APIs may expose only some of these settings, and reasoning
models may fix them.

> **In short.**
>
> - Generation settings choose the next token from the model's distribution.
> - Greedy is deterministic; sampling adds variety; top-k and top-p cut off
>   unlikely tokens; temperature sharpens ($T<1$) or flattens ($T>1$).
> - Low temperature for extraction and code, moderate with top-p for
>   writing.

## The generative AI project lifecycle {#generative-ai-project-lifecycle}

An LLM project moves through four stages, and later results often send you
back to an earlier one:

| Stage | Key decisions | Covered in |
|:------|:--------------|:-----------|
| **Scope** | Define the use case narrowly: which tasks, which inputs, what counts as success | This section |
| **Select** | Use an existing foundation model (the usual choice) or pre-train your own | Chapter \@ref(pre-training-and-scaling-large-language-models) |
| **Adapt and align** | Prompting first, then fine-tuning or PEFT, then alignment with human feedback; evaluate at every step | Chapters \@ref(instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation) and \@ref(alignment-human-feedback) |
| **Integrate** | Optimize for inference; add retrieval and tools to overcome model limits; deploy, monitor, and manage risks | Chapter \@ref(llm-applications) |

**Scoping matters most.** A model that must do many things needs to be larger
and more general than one that only extracts named entities from invoices. A
narrow scope makes model choice, evaluation, and risk assessment easier and
cheaper.

The inner loop is **adapt → evaluate → adapt**. Start with prompt engineering
and in-context learning. Measure against a held-out evaluation set. Fine-tune
only if prompting falls short. Then return to prompting with the tuned model.

### What each lever costs

The levers differ sharply in what they change, how long they take, and the
skill they demand. That is why the usual order is cheapest first:

| | Pre-training | Prompting | Fine-tuning / PEFT | Alignment (RLHF, DPO) | Compression |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **What changes** | All weights, plus the architecture, tokenizer, and context length | Nothing in the model; only the input | All weights, or small adapter weights (Section \@ref(peft)) | Weights or adapters, steered by preference data | Model size or precision: pruning, quantization, distillation |
| **Data needed** | A very large general or domain corpus | None, or a few examples in the prompt | Hundreds to many thousands of labeled task examples | Preference comparisons from humans or AI, often with a reward model | Little: a calibration set, or teacher outputs for distillation |
| **Training time** | Weeks to months on large clusters | None | Minutes to days | Similar to fine-tuning or longer | None to hours; distillation is a full training run |
| **Objective** | Next-token prediction on broad text | Better task performance | Better task performance on a specific task or domain | Match human preferences (helpful, honest, harmless) | Cheaper, faster inference |
| **Expertise** | High | Low | Medium | Medium to high | Medium |

Read the table across, not down. Moving right from prompting adds data
requirements, training cost, and the risk of degrading general abilities
(catastrophic forgetting). A lever is worth its cost only when the cheaper
ones have been measured and fall short.

> **Current practice (October 2026).** The time ranges are rough orders of
> magnitude; they depend on model size, data size, and hardware. Few teams
> pre-train their own LLM: they start from an open-weight or API model. Most
> alignment beyond the vendor's own now uses DPO or similar offline methods
> (Chapter \@ref(alignment-human-feedback)) rather than a full RLHF loop, which
> moves its expertise closer to that of fine-tuning.

Even a well-adapted model invents information when unsure and is unreliable
at exact computation. It also knows nothing after its training cut-off.
Production systems therefore add retrieval, tools, and verification around the
model; see Chapter \@ref(llm-applications).

> **In short.**
>
> - Scope, select, adapt and align, integrate, with evaluation throughout.
> - A narrow scope makes every later step easier.
> - Use the levers cheapest first: prompting, then fine-tuning, then
>   alignment; pre-train only in rare cases.

## Key takeaways

The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines:

- **What:** an LLM predicts the next token; most text tasks reduce to that.
- **How:** transformers replaced recurrence with attention, which is
  parallel, direct, and quadratic in length.
- **Shapes:** encoder, decoder, and encoder–decoder models suit different
  tasks.
- **Steering:** prompts and in-context examples shape what it does;
  generation settings shape how it samples.
- **Process:** scope narrowly, start from an existing model, adapt cheapest
  first, and evaluate throughout.

## Interview checkpoints

- **Why did transformers replace RNNs?** Parallel training across positions,
  and direct attention between any two tokens instead of a long chain of
  recurrent steps.
- **Write the attention formula. Why the $\sqrt{d_k}$?**
  $\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$. Without scaling, large dot products
  saturate the softmax and shrink the gradients.
- **What are Q, K, and V?** Learned projections of each token: what it is
  looking for (query), what it offers to be matched on (key), and the content
  it passes on when attended to (value).
- **Why multi-head attention?** Several heads can capture different relations
  in parallel at the same total cost.
- **Why does attention need positional information?** Attention treats its
  inputs as an unordered set; positional encodings or RoPE inject word order.
- **What does causal masking do?** It stops each decoder position from seeing
  future tokens, so training matches left-to-right generation.
- **What is the complexity of self-attention in sequence length?**
  Quadratic, $O(n^2)$.
- **Top-k vs. top-p?** Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. Top-p keeps a
  variable number whose cumulative probability reaches $p$.
- **What does temperature do?** It divides the logits before the softmax.
  Lower values sharpen the distribution; higher values flatten it.
- **Zero-shot vs. few-shot? When do you move to fine-tuning?** Few-shot
  includes solved examples in the prompt. Move on when a handful of examples
  does not reach the target performance, or when context or cost limits bite.
